feedback: If a learner marks the dart frog's colour as camouflage: 'Bright colour here ADVERTISES toxicity as a warning — the opposite of camouflage, which hides.'
Reinforce that both hiding and warning are different routes to the same goal of survival.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can distinguish the opposite strategies of hiding versus advertising, and connect real animals to their adaptation, benefit and layer.
learnerActions: Match each adaptation to the benefit it provides (camouflage→hide, warning colour→deter, prehensile tail→grip, beak→reach food, nocturnal→avoid predators/find food, for some avoid heat).
Answer a contrast question: given a described animal, decide whether it survives by HIDING (camouflage) or by being SEEN (warning colours), and explain why.
Name a specific animal for each adaptation and its rainforest layer.
activities.title: Match and contrast end-check

feedback: Target answer: the bright colour is a WARNING, not a mistake; it says 'I'm poisonous — don't eat me' so predators learn, or instinctively tend, to avoid it, the opposite of a camouflaged leaf insect or tree frog that hides by blending in.
If the learner can describe a feature but not its survival job, ask 'what problem does this feature solve?' (grip, reach, hide, warn).
activities.intendedInsight: Bright warning colour advertises toxicity (aposematism) so predators learn, or instinctively tend, to leave it alone — the opposite strategy to camouflage, which hides. One animal survives by being SEEN, one by being HIDDEN.
learnerActions: Consider: a poison dart frog is bright, shining red — one of the easiest things to spot in the forest. Explain why a frog would be coloured that way when it makes it so easy to see.
Explain how that is different from a leaf insect's dull, blending colours.
Answer the extension: what will a predator do next time it sees a bright frog after once eating one and getting sick, and how does that protect other frogs?
Discuss: if a harmless frog were also bright red but NOT poisonous, could that still help it? Why?
activities.title: Explain the dart frog paradox (discussion probe)
